title: Fair-price model for flats, with diagnostics and regularisation
summary: Build an explainable price model for 3,000 resale flats: log-price OLS you can read as % effects, residual and multicollinearity diagnostics, a scikit-learn pipeline with cross-validation, Ridge/Lasso on an expanded feature set, and an 'overpriced listing' flag.
business: A property portal covering Bengaluru and Pune wants a **'fair price' badge** on resale listings. Product asks two things: **what drives the price of a flat (and by how much), and which new listings are priced more than 15% above what comparable flats sell for?** Sellers will challenge the badge, so the model must be explainable in rupees and percentages, and its typical error must be stated honestly in ₹ lakh.

dataset.name: Synthetic resale-flat transactions (3,000 rows)
dataset.how: Generated in step 1 with `numpy.random.default_rng(11)`: city, locality, super built-up and carpet area (sq ft), bedrooms, age, floor, distance to metro (km), covered parking and sale price in ₹ lakh. Price is built multiplicatively (so log-price is linear) with noise; carpet area is deliberately almost collinear with super area.

steps.title: Generate the transactions
steps.detail: Prices in real estate are multiplicative: a good locality raises the price of a big flat by more rupees than a small one. So we generate log-price as a linear function plus noise. Carpet area is roughly 75% of super built-up area, which will create a multicollinearity problem you will diagnose in step 4.
steps.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import het_breuschpagan
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, KFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler, PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, RidgeCV, LassoCV
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_absolute_percentage_error

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
n = 3000
loc = {"Whitefield": ("Bengaluru", 0.00), "Indiranagar": ("Bengaluru", 0.45), "Electronic City": ("Bengaluru", -0.20),
       "Hinjewadi": ("Pune", -0.15), "Kothrud": ("Pune", 0.20), "Baner": ("Pune", 0.10)}
locality = rng.choice(list(loc), n)
area = np.round(rng.normal(1250, 350, n).clip(450, 2800))
beds = np.clip(np.round(area / 520 + rng.normal(0, 0.5, n)), 1, 5).astype(int)
age = rng.integers(0, 30, n)
floor = rng.integers(0, 25, n)
metro = np.round(rng.gamma(2, 1.5, n), 2)
parking = (rng.random(n) < 0.7).astype(int)
log_price = (np.log(0.09) + 0.95 * np.log(area) + np.array([loc[l][1] for l in locality])
             - 0.012 * age + 0.004 * floor - 0.035 * metro + 0.06 * parking + 0.02 * beds
             + rng.normal(0, 0.07, n))
flats = pd.DataFrame({"city": [loc[l][0] for l in locality], "locality": locality, "area": area,
                      "carpet": np.round(area * rng.normal(0.75, 0.01, n)), "beds": beds, "age": age,
                      "floor": floor, "metro_km": metro, "parking": parking,
                      "price_lakh": np.round(np.exp(log_price), 2)})
print(flats.describe().round(2))

steps.title: Explore: skew, correlations and the case for log-price
steps.detail: Plot the price distribution: it is right-skewed, and its spread grows with area. A log transform makes it roughly symmetric and turns multiplicative effects into additive ones, so a coefficient of 0.05 reads as ≈ +5%. Check correlations too: if two inputs correlate above 0.95, expect unstable coefficients.
steps.code:
flats["log_price"] = np.log(flats["price_lakh"])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4))
ax[0].hist(flats["price_lakh"], bins=50); ax[0].set_title("Price (₹ lakh)")
ax[1].hist(flats["log_price"], bins=50); ax[1].set_title("log(price)")
ax[2].scatter(flats["area"], flats["price_lakh"], s=4, alpha=0.4); ax[2].set_xlabel("sq ft"); ax[2].set_title("Price vs area")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig("flat_eda.png", dpi=100); plt.close()
print(flats.select_dtypes("number").corr().round(2)["log_price"].sort_values())
print("corr(area, carpet) =", round(flats["area"].corr(flats["carpet"]), 3))

steps.title: Baseline OLS with statsmodels and % interpretation
steps.detail: Hold out a test set first (20%), then fit OLS on the training data with a formula: `np.log(area)` gives an **elasticity** (a 1% bigger flat costs about b% more) and `C(locality)` creates dummies against a reference locality. Convert other coefficients into % effects with `100*(exp(b) − 1)`. Read the summary for coefficient signs, confidence intervals and adjusted R².
steps.code:
train, test = train_test_split(flats, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)
ols = smf.ols("log_price ~ np.log(area) + C(locality) + beds + age + floor + metro_km + parking", data=train).fit()
print(ols.summary().tables[1])
eff = (100 * (np.exp(ols.params) - 1)).round(2)
print("Effect in % per unit:\n", eff.drop(["Intercept", "np.log(area)"]))
print(f"Area elasticity: {ols.params['np.log(area)']:.2f}; adj R2 = {ols.rsquared_adj:.3f}")

steps.title: Diagnostics: residuals, heteroscedasticity and multicollinearity
steps.detail: Check the assumptions that make OLS intervals trustworthy. A residual-vs-fitted plot should look like a shapeless band; a Q–Q plot should be close to the line; the **Breusch–Pagan** test checks for variance that grows with the fit. Then add `carpet` to the model and compute **VIFs**: values above 10 mean the coefficient for area is now being shared with carpet and becomes unstable, so drop one of them.
steps.code:
import scipy.stats as st
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
ax[0].scatter(ols.fittedvalues, ols.resid, s=4, alpha=0.4); ax[0].axhline(0, color="k"); ax[0].set_title("Residuals vs fitted")
st.probplot(ols.resid, plot=ax[1]); ax[1].set_title("Q-Q plot of residuals")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig("flat_diagnostics.png", dpi=100); plt.close()
bp = het_breuschpagan(ols.resid, ols.model.exog)
print(f"Breusch-Pagan p = {bp[1]:.3f}")
X = train[["area", "carpet", "beds", "age", "floor", "metro_km", "parking"]].assign(const=1.0)
vif = pd.Series([variance_inflation_factor(X.values, i) for i in range(X.shape[1])], index=X.columns)
print(vif.drop("const").round(1))
both = smf.ols("log_price ~ np.log(area) + np.log(carpet) + C(locality) + beds + age + floor + metro_km + parking", data=train).fit()
print("With carpet too:", both.params[["np.log(area)", "np.log(carpet)"]].round(2).to_dict(),
      "std errors:", both.bse[["np.log(area)", "np.log(carpet)"]].round(2).to_dict())

steps.title: Rebuild as a scikit-learn pipeline with cross-validation
steps.detail: For production you want one object that does encoding, scaling and fitting, so the exact same transformations run at training and prediction time and nothing leaks across CV folds. A `ColumnTransformer` one-hot encodes locality and scales numbers; `cross_val_score` with 5 folds gives a mean and spread of RMSE on log-price, which is a more honest estimate than a single split.
steps.code:
num = ["area", "beds", "age", "floor", "metro_km", "parking"]
cat_cols = ["locality"]
Xtr, ytr = train[num + cat_cols].copy(), train["log_price"]
Xte, yte = test[num + cat_cols].copy(), test["log_price"]
Xtr["area"], Xte["area"] = np.log(Xtr["area"]), np.log(Xte["area"])
pre = ColumnTransformer([("num", StandardScaler(), num), ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop="first"), cat_cols)])
cv = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
lin = Pipeline([("pre", pre), ("model", LinearRegression())])
s = -cross_val_score(lin, Xtr, ytr, cv=cv, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
print(f"Linear CV RMSE (log) = {s.mean():.4f} ± {s.std():.4f}")

steps.title: Expand features, then regularise with Ridge and Lasso
steps.detail: Add all pairwise interactions (does a metro station matter more in Indiranagar?). This multiplies the number of features and invites overfitting; **Ridge** shrinks all coefficients, **Lasso** sets unhelpful ones to exactly zero. `RidgeCV`/`LassoCV` pick the penalty by internal CV. Compare all three with the same outer folds and keep the simplest model within one standard error of the best.
steps.code:
pre_poly = ColumnTransformer([("num", Pipeline([("poly", PolynomialFeatures(2, include_bias=False)), ("sc", StandardScaler())]), num),
                              ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop="first"), cat_cols)])
models = {"poly + OLS": LinearRegression(), "poly + Ridge": RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-3, 3, 25)),
          "poly + Lasso": LassoCV(alphas=np.logspace(-5, -1, 20), max_iter=20000)}
res = {"linear": s}
for name, m in models.items():
    res[name] = -cross_val_score(Pipeline([("pre", pre_poly), ("model", m)]), Xtr, ytr, cv=cv, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
print(pd.DataFrame({k: [v.mean(), v.std()] for k, v in res.items()}, index=["cv_rmse", "sd"]).T.round(4))
lasso = Pipeline([("pre", pre_poly), ("model", models["poly + Lasso"])]).fit(Xtr, ytr)
coef = lasso.named_steps["model"].coef_
print(f"Lasso kept {np.sum(coef != 0)} of {coef.size} features (alpha = {lasso.named_steps['model'].alpha_:.5f})")

steps.title: Evaluate on the test set in rupees
steps.detail: Fit the chosen model on all training data and score the untouched test set once. Back-transform to ₹ lakh with `exp`, multiplied by a **smearing factor** (the mean of exp(residuals)) because exp of the mean log is the median, not the mean, price. Report MAE in ₹ lakh and MAPE, and look at errors by locality: a model that is great on average can still be biased for one neighbourhood.
steps.code:
final = lin.fit(Xtr, ytr)
smear = np.mean(np.exp(ytr - final.predict(Xtr)))
pred = np.exp(final.predict(Xte)) * smear
actual = test["price_lakh"].to_numpy()
print(f"Test MAE ₹{mean_absolute_error(actual, pred):.2f} lakh, MAPE {100 * mean_absolute_percentage_error(actual, pred):.1f}% (smearing {smear:.4f})")
err = pd.DataFrame({"locality": test["locality"], "pct_err": 100 * (pred - actual) / actual})
print(err.groupby("locality")["pct_err"].agg(["mean", "std"]).round(2))

steps.title: Flag overpriced listings
steps.detail: Simulate 500 new listings (sellers usually ask a premium, a few ask a lot) and flag those whose asking price exceeds the fair price by more than 15%. Because the model's typical error is around ±5–6%, a 15% threshold keeps false accusations rare; quantify that by checking how often a *fairly* priced flat would cross it. Show the flagged listings with their fair-price range.
steps.code:
new = flats.sample(500, random_state=5).reset_index(drop=True)
premium = np.where(rng.random(500) < 0.15, rng.uniform(1.2, 1.45, 500), rng.normal(1.04, 0.05, 500))
new["asking_lakh"] = np.round(new["price_lakh"] * premium, 2)
Xn = new[num + cat_cols].copy(); Xn["area"] = np.log(Xn["area"])
new["fair_lakh"] = np.exp(final.predict(Xn)) * smear
new["gap_%"] = 100 * (new["asking_lakh"] / new["fair_lakh"] - 1)
flag = new["gap_%"] > 15
print(f"Flagged {flag.sum()} of 500 listings as >15% above fair price")
print(new.loc[flag, ["locality", "area", "beds", "asking_lakh", "fair_lakh", "gap_%"]].head(8).round(1))
false_flag = np.mean(np.exp(yte - final.predict(Xte)) / smear > 1.15)
print(f"Share of fairly priced test flats that would be flagged: {false_flag:.1%}")

deliverables: A coefficient table translated into plain English: '+1 km from metro ≈ −3.4% price', '10% more area ≈ +9.5% price', locality premiums in %.
A diagnostics page: residual and Q–Q plots, Breusch–Pagan result and the VIF table, with the decision you took on carpet area.
A model comparison table (linear vs polynomial OLS vs Ridge vs Lasso) with CV RMSE ± SD and the chosen model justified.
Test-set MAE in ₹ lakh and MAPE, plus a list of flagged listings with fair-price estimates.

rubric.good: Log-price justified by skew and multiplicative effects; log-area interpreted as an elasticity.
Residual plots, heteroscedasticity test and VIF all run and interpreted; collinear feature handled.
Test set held out from the start; preprocessing inside the pipeline; model chosen on CV only.
Ridge/Lasso penalties picked by CV; explains why the simpler model wins when scores tie.
Errors reported in ₹ lakh with smearing; the 15% flag threshold is justified against model error.

extensions: Replace the point estimate with a prediction interval (statsmodels `get_prediction`) and only flag listings whose asking price is above the 90% upper bound.
Add a gradient boosting regressor and check whether it beats the linear model by more than one CV standard error; discuss the explainability trade-off.
Fit a mixed model or target-encode 50 micro-localities and compare with one-hot encoding under cross-validation.
